paper_title: Agent-R$^2$: Scaling Agents for Realistic Productivity Work via Real-Source Data Synthesis

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language models have made rapid progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, raising expectations for agents that can take over realistic productivity work from humans. However, current agents still struggle to finish such tasks, where success requires following long-horizon professional workflows, understanding heterogeneous file contexts, and producing usable deliverables under fine-grained requirements. A key bottleneck is the lack of scalable post-training data that reflects real work intent, authentic file environments, and deliverable-level evaluation. To close this gap, we introduce Agent-R$^2$, a $\textbf{r}$eal-source data synthesis framework that scales training data for $\textbf{r}$ealistic productivity work. Instead of relying on manually specified workflows or LLM-generated files, Agent-R$^2$ grounds synthesis throughout the pipeline in real occupational seeds, corpus-derived workflow evidence, and authentic web-sourced files. From 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R$^2$ distills 4k task instances that pair real multi-format attachments with fine-grained, deliverable-level rubrics. On this data, we train Agent-R$^2$-4B via supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learning, improving both end-to-end productivity performance and file-grounded reasoning. Trained on only 4k instances, Agent-R$^2$-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 on both GDPval (51.0$\%$ vs. 48.0$\%$) and OfficeQA (14.8$\%$ vs. 13.8$\%$). Further analysis shows that Agent-R$^2$ mitigates shortcut behavior, where agents produce superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Large language models have made remarkable progress in agentic reasoning and tool use, enabling agents to plan, interact with environments, and solve increasingly open-ended tasks (Yao et al. 2023; Schick et al. 2023; Zhou et al. 2024). These advances raise the expectation that agents can take over realistic productivity work from humans. Such work is economically valuable but demanding: it involves longhorizon professional workflows, where agents must understand professional contexts, gather and integrate evidence from heterogeneous digital artifacts, invoke the necessary tools, and ultimately deliver usable work products such as analytical reports, spreadsheets, presentations, and structured documents. Code is available at https://github.com/ZJU-REAL/Agent-R2 Figure 1: GDPval Pass@1 comparison. Agent-R2-4B improves the Qwen3-4B-Thinking base model by 18.6 points and surpasses several larger open-source baselines. However, current agents still fall short on such work. First, real professional workflows involve interdependent steps, implicit domain conventions, and evolving intermediate states, so models miss critical operations or fail to adapt based on feedback. Second, real file contexts are heterogeneous and messy: models must integrate evidence across artifacts with different formats, layouts, and levels of completeness, and often misread content or overlook cross-file dependencies. Third, real deliverables must satisfy fine-grained requirements over factual consistency, evidence coverage, structure, formatting, and practical usability; producing an output file is not the same as meeting deliverable standards. Mastering all three demands at once is precisely what current training data fails to teach. Existing training data targets these capabilities only in instruction following (Xu et al. 2025a; Guo isolation: et al. 2025), multidisciplinary reasoning (Liu et al. 2025), document-grounded question answering (Tanaka et al. 2023; Zhang et al. 2026a), or generation of single deliverable type such as presentations and spreadsheets (Zheng et al. 2025, 2026; Chi et al. 2026). While effective in their respective settings, these data sources do not provide end-to-end supervision that jointly covers real work objectives, cross-file evidence, professional workflow execution, and deliverable constraints. What is missing, we argue, is not more data but data that reflects real work: real intents, authentic files, and deliverable-level standards. Such data is hard to fabricate: manually authored workflows do not scale, and LLM-generated files lack the layouts, gaps, and cross-file references of real documents. To address this data bottleneck, we introduce Agent-R2, real-source data synthesis framework that grounds every stage of synthesis in real sources through three-stage pipeline. First, rather than relying on manually authored workflows as in recent benchmark construction (Patwardhan et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2026), Agent-R2 mines file-oriented workflow blueprints from web corpora using occupational activity seeds, improving both realism and scalability. Second, it searches for and verifies public files that support each workflow, retaining the heterogeneous formats, layouts, incomplete structures, and cross-file dependencies of realistic digital work. Third, it synthesizes user instructions and fine-grained rubrics from the verified workflow-file contexts: the instructions require complex deliverables involving evidence gathering, reasoning, file operations, and artifact construction, while the rubrics specify detailed criteria for evidence grounding, analytical correctness, and deliverable quality. Starting from 10k web-corpus candidates, Agent-R2 produces 4k highquality training instances. We train Agent-R2-4B on the synthesized data using supervised fine-tuning followed by rubric-based reinforcement learning. The reinforcement learning stage optimizes the model in the persistent sandbox with outcome rewards: each generated deliverable is evaluated against its fine-grained rubric, which encourages the model to satisfy evidence, reasoning, and artifact-quality requirements rather than merely produce an output file. Trained on only 4k synthesized instances, Agent-R2-4B reaches 51.0% Pass@1 on the full GDPval set (Figure 1), improving the base model by 18.6 points and surpassing Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507 (48.0%) and Qwen3-VL-235B-A22B-Thinking (49.7%). The gains transfer to document-grounded reasoning on OfficeQA: Agent-R2-4B improves the base model from 2.2% to 14.8% Pass@1 and again surpasses Qwen3-235BA22B-Thinking-2507 (13.8%). Behavioral analysis further shows that training on rubric-scored real-source data mitigates shortcut behavior, general failure mode where agents emit superficially plausible deliverables before sufficiently grounding, constructing, or verifying them, while promoting sustained exploration. Our contributions are summarized as follows: We introduce Agent-R2, data synthesis framework that grounds workflow extraction, file collection, and instruction-rubric synthesis in real sources, scaling training data for realistic productivity work. We synthesize 4k high-quality productivity-work instances with authentic multi-format attachments and finegrained rubrics, and train Agent-R2-4B with SFT and rubric-based RL. Agent-R2-4B surpasses Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking2507 on GDPval and OfficeQA; further analysis indicates that the training mitigates shortcut behavior while promoting sustained exploration.

3.1 Pipeline
In this section, we detail the data synthesis pipeline of
Agent-R2. The overall pipeline is illustrated in Figure 2. The
prompts used in each stage are provided in the supplementary
material.
sections.content: Figure 2: Agent-R2 data synthesis pipeline. The framework extracts file-oriented workflow blueprints from real web-corpus evidence, retrieves and verifies public attachments, and synthesizes instructions, rubrics, and references in sandbox. Workflow Extraction. Prior work observes that raw web text can encode implicit tool-use workflows (Xu et al. 2026b). Inspired by this observation, we further treat web corpora as natural source of workflow evidence for realistic productivity work and focus on file-oriented workflows, where completing the work requires locating, reading, editing, or producing file artifacts. By leveraging broad web corpora, Agent-R2 enables scalable workflow construction and avoids the limited scalability of manually curated workflows (Patwardhan et al. 2025; Chen et al. 2026). We begin with web corpus and occupational activity seeds G. These seeds can be drawn from different occupational resources; in this work, we use seeds from O*NET. For the web corpus, we use samples from the DLR-Web dataset (Attention1115 2025) used by DESIGNER (Liu et al. 2025), which are filtered from FineFineWeb (m-a-p 2025). Each segment has corpus-provided discipline metadata, which we map to an occupational category to select the corresponding seeds from G. For each segment, we perform workflow extraction under two filtering criteria: workflow filtering and file-oriented filtering. segment that satisfies both criteria is converted into workflow blueprint, information dependencies, required file types, and expected outputs, where the extraction is performed by Qwen3.6-Plus as the synthesis model πsyn: = {w Filtered(C), πsyn( c, G)}. Attachment Searching. Given the workflow blueprints W, we retrieve public file artifacts and construct candidate file sets. Unlike prior settings built on large amounts of LLMgenerated synthetic files (Ge et al. 2026), we ground each task in authentic files retrieved from the web, guided by cues that the extracted workflows provide; such files preserve the natural complexity of file structures, layouts, and cross-file evidence. For each workflow w, we use πsyn to run multiturn search-and-verification loop. At each turn, it generates search query conditioned on the workflow, required file types, previous queries, and prior search results, and executes web_search to obtain results that include titles and snippets. For each result, it first checks its title and snippet for workflow relevance; promising candidates are then downloaded and inspected with bash and view_image to check key parts such as cover pages and tables of contents. Files verified as relevant to the workflow are retained in Fc; to control download latency and construction overhead, we discard files longer than 50 pages or larger than 2 MB. The loop stops when the retained files jointly satisfy the information and operation needs of w, or the maximum number of search turns is reached. The instruction specifies the expected deliverable, while the rubric ties success criteria to file-level evidence and constraints. We then use Claude-Opus-4.5 as the expert policy πexp to solve the synthesized task in the sandbox. The resulting files are kept as reference files Fr for evaluation and judging. Along with the deliverable, we also record the expert trajectory τ , which captures the tool interactions used to inspect files, execute operations, and construct the final output. sections.title:
4.1 Training Framework
Using the synthesized task set D and filtered expert trajec-
tories Z, we train Qwen3-4B-Thinking-2507 in two stages:
supervised fine-tuning and rubric-based reinforcement learn-
ing (Huang et al. 2025; Gunjal et al. 2025). SFT teaches the
model to follow expert trajectories, inspect files, and per-
form tool-based operations for deliverable construction. RL
further optimizes the policy for rubric-scored outcome qual-
ity, encouraging error recovery and stronger satisfaction of
task requirements. We split the data into 3k instances for SFT
and 1k tasks for RL, with no task overlap.
sections.content: Rubric-Based Reinforcement Learning. Starting from the SFT model, we optimize the policy with GRPO (Shao et al. 2024) in the persistent sandbox environment, as illustrated in Figure 3. Since agent-as-a-judge evaluation requires additional interactive tool use and is inefficient during RL training, we use Qwen3.6-Plus as an MLLM-as-ajudge (Chen et al. 2024) for outcome scoring. After task completion, the generated deliverable, relevant file evidence, and reference files are converted into model-consumable representations: .pdf, .pptx, and .docx files are rendered into images, while .xlsx files are represented by recalculated values and formulas in Markdown together with rendered page images, preserving both cell-level content and visual layout. The judge then scores the result against the synthesized rubric and reference files. To avoid inducing tool-specific calling preferences, we use only outcome reward and do not add explicit penalties for intermediate tool-call errors. sections.title:
4.4 Analysis
We further analyze how SFT and RL reshape the model’s
behavior, and show that our synthesized data help mitigate
shortcut behavior through grounded exploration and deliver-
able verification.
sections.content: SFT Encourages Sustained Exploration. The left panel of Figure 4 shows that SFT substantially increases the models exploratory behavior. The base model makes only 6.7 tool-call steps and 2.88 tool-call errors per sample on average. Such limited interaction suggests that the base model often stops active exploration after encountering early parsing, execution, or file-handling errors, and instead rushes to construct deliverables with insufficient grounding. AgentR2-4B-SFT increases the average number of tool-call steps to 39.0, with tool-call errors also increasing to 16.3. This shift indicates that SFT teaches the model to inspect files more actively, execute multi-step workflows, and continue attempting corrections after errors. Although limited model capacity and realistic environmental complexity lead to more errors, the longer exploration process ultimately guides the model toward more complete deliverables. Due to limited generalization, not every exploration attempt produces successful deliverable, as reflected by the completion-rate drop from 86.8% to 78.2%, which limits the potential gain. However, this shapes more proactive behavior pattern and lays the foundation for subsequent RL optimization. RL Improves Reliable and High-Quality Completion. RL preserves the exploratory behavior introduced by SFT and turns it into more reliable task completion. Figure 4(left) shows that Agent-R2-4B raises the completion rate to 90.9%, above both the base and SFT variants. On the one hand, it averages 33.1 tool-call steps, far above the base models 6.7, indicating that it does not fall back to sparse inspection and premature output. On the other hand, tool-call errors decrease from 16.3 under SFT to 12.9, suggesting that rubric-based RL helps the model recover from errors, explore more efficiently, and generalize better in complex environments. Furthermore, the completion quality improves. Figure 4(right) compares Agent-R2-4B with the SFT-only variant on GDPval tasks that both models complete successfully. The comparison shows that RL wins more often than SFT on both office and nonoffice tasks, indicating that rubric-based RL improves not only completion rate but also the quality of deliverables. Mitigating Shortcut Behavior Drives Improvement. We define effective steps as tool-call steps that do not result in errors, which to some extent reflect exploration and completion depth. In Figure 5, we observe that effective steps positively correlate with GDPval Pass@1. Across model scales, agents with few effective steps tend to stop before sufficient grounding or verification, producing plausible artifacts without adequate evidence extraction or computation. We refer to this failure mode as shortcut behavior. Agent-R2 mitigates this failure mode through two-stage SFT and rubric-based RL on the synthesized 4k data; in contrast, the 4B base model shows shallow interaction and low performance. sections.content: real-world interactive environments, emphasizing live operations, sustained exploration, and feedback-driven progress. Workspace-Bench (Tang et al. 2026) and EnterpriseClawBench (Zhong et al. 2026) focus on workspace and enterprise settings, where agents must reason over heterogeneous files, business artifacts, and workplace-specific context. Data Synthesis for Agent Post-Training. Synthesizing post-training data has become an important direction for improving agent capabilities. Existing work scales tool-use trajectories and executable environments from corpora, programs, or workflow templates (Xu et al. 2026b; Song et al. 2026; Xu et al. 2026a; Dong et al. 2026), or replay web tutorials as verified GUI trajectories (Xu et al. 2025b). These methods are effective for scaling tool-use data, but they mainly target specific tools with predefined interfaces rather than more general tools such as terminals, which offer broader applicability for realistic productivity work. Recent data synthesis for terminal agents improves verifiability by generating command-line environments, tasks, or skills (Gandhi et al. 2026; Cheng et al. 2026; Hua et al. 2026). However, these settings mainly focus on structured text files and rarely involve structurally complex office files commonly used in professional productivity work. Studies based on office files mainly focus on document-grounded question answering and analysis (Zhang et al. 2026a; Qiao et al. 2026; Zhang et al. 2025; Chi et al. 2026) or single-type file generation (Zheng et al. 2025, 2026). In contrast, Agent-R2 grounds task synthesis in real occupational workflows and authentic multi-format attachments, producing deliverable-oriented tasks together with fine-grained rubrics.

6 Conclusion
We introduced Agent-R2, a real-source data synthesis frame-
work that scales agents for realistic productivity work. Agent-
R2 constructs training instances grounded in real work-
flows and authentic files with fine-grained rubrics. Using
4k synthesized instances, we train Agent-R2-4B with SFT
and rubric-based RL. Experiments on GDPval and Of-
ficeQA show that Agent-R2-4B improves task completion
and file-grounded reasoning, outperforming several larger
open-source baselines. Behavioral analysis further shows that
Agent-R2-4B reduces shortcut behavior and improves com-
pletion reliability in complex productivity tasks.

sections.content: GDPval scores rely on an LLM judge, so we test whether our conclusions depend on judge stochasticity or on the choice of judge. We use two judge models, Gemini-3.1-Pro and DeepSeek-v4-Flash, and each judge independently evaluates the deliverables of Agent-R2-4B and Qwen3-235B-A22BThinking-2507 on all 220 GDPval tasks three times. Table 8 reports the range of Pass@1 across the three repeats. Per-task scores do vary between repeats, with median absolute difference of 3.2 and 3.1 points (mean 5.7 and 5.4) under the two judges, but these differences largely cancel in the aggregate score. Agent-R2-4B stays within 50.851.1 under Gemini-3.1-Pro, consistent with the 51.0 reported in Table 1, and within 51.752.3 under DeepSeek-v4-Flash. The two judges differ slightly in absolute scores but agree on relative quality, with per-task Pearson correlation of 0.93. Under both judges, the lowest score of Agent-R2-4B is above the highest score of Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking-2507, so Agent-R2-4B leads in all six evaluations. Note that this definition counts only genuine error signatures, so absolute counts differ slightly from Figure 5. Table 11 shows that from SFT to RL, almost the entire decrease comes from computation steps such as data processing, which drop from 11.9 to 7.3 per task. Attachment reading is unchanged, while deliverable writing and the build phase grow. As result, RL spends larger share of its effective steps on reading, writing, and checking the deliverable (40%48%). More steps do not mean better work. Within each model, longer trajectories score lower (per-task Spearman correlation 0.15 for SFT and 0.41 for RL), and the share of runs that hit the 100-step limit drops from 8.2% to 3.6%. Metric Definitions for Shortcut Analysis The following definitions are used for the trajectoryand deliverable-level analysis in Section 4.4. All statistics are computed automatically with rule-based matching on trajectories and deliverables. Error. tool call whose output contains genuine error signature, such as traceback, an error message, or missing file. Output on stderr without an error signature is not counted. Phases. The exploration phase precedes the first successful deliverable write; the build phase spans the first to the last successful write; the verification phase follows the last successful write. Numerical-error fix rate. The of numerical/data-logic error episodes that are subsequently fixed under the criterion above. This category includes indexing, value, type, arithmetic, and related computation exceptions. percentage Writing despite an unfixed error. deliverable is written before an error is fixed, with at most one intervening successful step. The reported rate is the percentage of build-phase error episodes that satisfy this condition. Re-checking the deliverable. The agent reopens or inspects the deliverable after successful write. The rate is measured over tasks with successful deliverable-writing operation. Placeholder text. The deliverable contains placeholder strings such as TBD, [insert . . . ], lorem, or placeholder. The rate is measured over tasks with reference attachments and an output deliverable. Error masking. The code that writes the deliverable catches exceptions and falls back to default value or pass. We report the percentage of tasks with successful deliverable-writing operation whose writer code matches this pattern. Traceable numbers. The share of distinct numbers in the output deliverables that can be found in the prompt or the attachments. We compute this share for each task with reference attachments and at least five distinct output numbers, then report the mean across eligible tasks.

sections.title: D Decontamination Audit
sections.content: Our training materials are collected from web corpora and online search, so we audit the synthesized tasks and their attachments for overlap with the evaluation benchmarks at four levels. File hashes and source URLs. Neither the SHA-256 hashes of our attachment files nor the source URLs we recovered overlap with any file in GDPval or OfficeQA. Source domains. Only 0.6% of our source domains appear in GDPval instructions, mostly broad public sources such as irs.gov. Near-duplicate documents. For each attachment, we compute the nearest-neighbor 5-gram MinHash Jaccard similarity to the benchmark documents. The average is 0.005 for GDPval (maximum 0.125) and 0.009 for OfficeQA (maximum 0.023). For reference, two different issues of the same U.S. Treasury Bulletin have similarity of 0.36. Instruction-level similarity. For each benchmark prompt, we compute the embedding cosine similarity to its nearest training instruction. The average is 0.43 for GDPval and 0.36 for OfficeQA. For GDPval, this is below the similarity between GDPval prompt and its nearest other GDPval prompt (0.46), and far below the similarity of paraphrase (0.93).

sections.title: E Data Details
sections.content: Retrieving real files does not by itself guarantee realistic tasks: topic-relevant attachments may differ in entities, dates, or assumptions, and synthesized rubrics may not be grounded in the files. This section brings together filtering decisions, synthesis statistics, manual quality audits, and data compliance and release details. E.1 Filtering Decisions and Data Attrition Each filtering step is implemented as structured decision that the prompts in Appendix require the model to output in JSON. For example, during workflow extraction only documents labeled "workflow": true are kept, and during attachment searching only files listed under "highly_relevant_files" are retained. Starting from 10k seed documents, about 2.2k are discarded at workflow extraction and about 3.8k during attachment searching and verification, leaving about 4k task instances. E.2 Semantic Similarity Across Synthesis Stages Figure 8 reports text similarity measured by Qwen3Embedding-4B across synthesis stages. The final instructions have low similarity to the seed tasks, with an average similarity of 0.33. E.3 Manual Quality Inspection We conduct manual audit of 100 examples from the retained synthesis set across three quality dimensions: workflow question alignment (86%), rubric-item validity (99.8%), and visual presentation (97%). Workflow and question construction are fully aligned in 86 examples, while the remaining 14 show partial alignment. In these cases, some questions use descriptive calculations in place of causal or simulation analysis, some omit key crossvalidation, and others omit or modify requested artifact. Despite these differences, all 14 examples remain topically consistent with their workflows, although topical consistency alone does not meet the criterion for full alignment. For rubric validity, two rubric items are inaccurate because repeated calculations produce incorrect numerical values. For visual presentation, the examples with room for improvement mainly contain sparse table or continuation pages and otherwise blank trailing pages with only footer. These presentation issues do not affect the overall readability of the deliverables. E.4 Cross-File Consistency and Task Feasibility We further manually evaluate the same 100 tasks along two additional dimensions. Cross-file consistency asks whether the attachments of task describe mutually compatible entities, dates, and assumptions. Feasibility asks whether the task can be completed from its instruction and attachments. Crossfile consistency reaches 95%, and task feasibility reaches 85%. Among the inconsistent tasks, one example mixes GPU specifications with data on ASIC Bitcoin miners. E.5 Rubric Grounding The manual audit finds that 99.8% of rubric items are valid. To measure how strongly rubrics depend on the attachments, we trace every specific number that appears in the training rubrics. Of these numbers, 41.9% appear in the instruction, 39.0% appear only in the attachments, and 19.1% appear in neither and must be computed. Most rubric numbers therefore cannot be checked from the instruction alone, so satisfying the rubric requires reading and processing the attached files.
